transcript.content: Hello. What brings you to the clinic today?

I spend so much time checking and rechecking how I look at the gym and before going out that it’s taking over my days. It has gotten to the point where it's completely taking over my schedule and I just can't seem to stop.
When you check your appearance, what is the main concern driving you to do so? Are you worried about your body weight and shape, a specific flaw in how you look, or is it a different kind of urge?

It's not really about my weight or body shape, but I'm obsessed with how crooked my face looks and how weird my jawline is from the side. I end up spending hours zooming in on photos and checking every mirror to try and hide those specific parts before anyone can see me.

Are these repetitive checking behaviors and worries strictly focused on your physical appearance, or do you also experience other repetitive rituals like excessive handwashing, checking locks, or needing things in a perfect order?
No, it's strictly about how I look. I don't have any rituals like handwashing or checking locks; all of my checking is just about fixing my hair, changing clothes, and trying to hide my face.
How long have you been experiencing these intense worries and checking behaviors regarding your face and jawline?

I’ve had some self-consciousness about my looks for a long time, but it got really severe recently. It escalated when my soccer teammates started posting high-resolution photos and workout videos of us on social media. Seeing myself frozen in those action shots made me start obsessing over how my face and jawline look from different angles.
How many months has this severe level of daily obsession and checking been going on?

I'm not entirely sure of the exact number of months, but it has definitely been building up over a while now. It really started getting out of hand once those photos and videos started going up online.
Do your friends, family, or teammates tell you that they don't notice anything wrong with your face or jawline, and if so, does their reassurance help ease your worries?

Yes, my friends and sister tell me they don't see anything wrong with my face or jawline at all, but their reassurance doesn't help at all. I still feel incredibly anxious and continue to spend hours zooming in on photos and obsessing over how crooked I look. No matter what they say, I just can't stop seeing it.
How much has this worry about your face and jawline affected your daily life, such as your ability to go to work, school, or hang out with friends?

It’s had a huge impact on my life because I’ve been missing work shifts and turning down hours because I get stuck checking myself. I’ve also been canceling soccer matches and salsa nights because I'm terrified of people seeing me from the wrong angle. Now, my sister and my friends are constantly bringing up how I’m never around anymore.
Do you worry that the crookedness of your face or jawline is caused by a medical illness or physical disease, or is your concern strictly about how it looks visually?

No, I don't worry about it being a medical illness or disease at all. My concern is strictly about how it looks visually because I'm just deeply self-conscious about how crooked my face looks and how weird my jawline appears from certain angles. It just makes me feel like I look completely wrong.
Can you estimate if this intense focus and worry about your face and jawline has been going on for at least six months?

Yes, it has definitely been going on for much longer than six months. It started as a long-standing self-consciousness about my appearance that I've had for years, and it has just gradually worsened over time to get this bad.

latest_inference.note: The patient exhibits a severe preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance (crooked face and jawline) that is not observable to others, accompanied by repetitive checking and camouflaging behaviors. This has persisted for over six months, causes significant social and occupational impairment, and is not driven by weight concerns or beliefs of a medical illness. In ICD-10, Body Dysmorphic Disorder is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder). Therefore, the candidate remains F45.2 and we can finalize the diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with symptoms highly characteristic of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (classified under F45.2 Hypochondriacal Disorder in ICD-10). They exhibit a persistent preoccupation with perceived, non-existent, or minimal defects in their physical appearance (crooked face and weird jawline). This is accompanied by repetitive behaviors (excessive mirror checking, zooming in on photos, and attempting to camouflage the perceived flaws) that are time-consuming and cause significant distress. The symptoms have been present for over six months, are not better explained by an eating disorder or another somatic/anxiety disorder, and have led to severe functional impairment in social and occupational domains.
